title: Marking & feedback
statement: A tutor marks a student paragraph. Watch the order an expert works in — read first, then the claim, the unsupported assertion, a light correction, the overclaim, the genuine strength, and finally feed-forward.

segments.text: fossil fuels are bad, and solar panels keep getting
. In 2010 solar was costly, but now
far more affordable — which proves it will soon

steps.title: Read it through first
steps.text: Before a single mark, read the whole piece for the writer’s intent. Marking is a response to meaning — not a spellcheck.

steps.title: Find the claim
steps.text: Underline the central claim so you both know what is being argued. Nothing is “wrong” yet — you are orienting attention.

steps.title: Question unsupported assertions
steps.text: Ring a claim that rests on nobody in particular and ask for a source in the margin. A question invites evidence rather than scolding.

steps.title: Correct slips lightly
steps.text: Show the fix for a mechanical error — strike it, write the correction above. Do not rewrite their work for them.

steps.title: Challenge the leap in reasoning
steps.text: Ring the overclaim and name the gap in logic. Push on the argument, not the person.

steps.title: Credit what works
steps.text: Tick the genuine strength and say why. Specific praise tells the writer what to keep — feedback is not only correction.

steps.title: End with feed-forward
steps.text: Close with the strength, then one or two specific, actionable next steps. Feed-forward is the part that changes the next draft.

feedForward.text: You have a real strength in the cost trend. Two next steps: (1) replace “everyone knows” with a cited source; (2) soften “the best solution … replace everything” to a claim you can defend.
